author: Ethan Brooks
title: Tuchel & England: Politics & Symbolism at Euro 2024
text:
The St George’s Cross and a Nation’s Identity Crisis: Football Caught in the Crossfire Into this “stinking cheese dream of contested symbolisms,” as the source text describes it, steps Thomas Tuchel’s England team. Refreshed after a summer slump, they face Andorra this Saturday and Serbia next Tuesday.While sporting questions – Elliot Anderson’s midfield potential and Tuchel’s tactical approach – remain relevant, the broader context looms large. This is a pivotal moment for the team to take the field under a flag laden with complex and often contradictory meanings.
English football, historically resistant to intellectualism and focused on the bottom line, has often shied away from these conversations. The priority, as one industry insider explained, is maintaining “vibes,” selling “disposable barbecues,” and filling “pub gardens.” The usual platitudes – “no greater honour,” “play for the shirt” – are readily deployed to deflect deeper scrutiny.
Tuchel himself has signaled a desire to “depoliticise” the England team, declaring himself a “head coach, not a manager” and expressing distaste for “sport-politics.” he even suggested his foreignness provides a degree of insulation from such issues. While understandable,this stance effectively asserts that his team will “stand for nothing outside itself,” focusing solely on playing and winning. Though, as the text points out, even this attempt at neutrality carries its own inherent meaning.
The very act of trying to be apolitical is a political statement, particularly within the intensely symbolic realm of football. As Roland Barthes argued, meaning inevitably finds a way, even in the face of deliberate attempts to strip it away.
The question of who gets to define the meaning of the England flag is paramount. Is it the fan painting it on her cheek,the players walking out onto the pitch,or the individual defacing a zebra crossing at 3 a.m.? The source text wryly notes the discomfort of Keir Starmer, seemingly forced to endorse a bizarre meal of roast chicken, custard, and Haribo bhuna as a demonstration of his understanding.
Ultimately,the England team represents more than just athletic prowess; they embody an idea. The flag they play under carries connotations they did not create and may not even share. this, the author suggests, is perhaps England’s “original sin”: a lack of a clear, unifying idea, replaced by “empty and unfocused fervour.”
However, the author argues, recoiling from defining these symbols only makes them more vulnerable to appropriation. the Lionesses’ success over the summer demonstrated that Englishness can be expressed positively, as a celebration of unity, diversity, and shared values. Like the flags of Palestine, Ukraine, or the Pride movement, the St George’s Cross can be a symbol of agency and inclusivity.
Acknowledging the political nature of international football is crucial, even if it’s “tiring to have to keep having these arguments.” In a society “stripped to a husk,” reduced to “howling at symbols,” those symbols take on immense importance. When symbols are all that remain,they matter a great deal.
as England prepares for upcoming matches against Andorra and serbia, the ubiquitous presence of the St George’s Cross has taken on a troubling new dimension, exposing deep fissures in national identity and raising uncomfortable questions about the politicization of football.
The familiar emblem, onc a symbol of national pride, is now appearing in increasingly unsettling contexts. Reports indicate the crosses are being daubed on Islamic centers in Basildon, defacing Chinese takeaways in York, and even displayed by individuals shouting at hotels from mini-roundabouts. Online, they are readily available for purchase – retailing for as little as £2.36 on Temu,with options ranging from car window size to large enough to scrawl slogans like “GET OFF MY LAND.”
